definition: The process of splitting long documents or text into smaller segments for processing, indexing, or inclusion in a model's context.
details: Chunking strategy (size, overlap, and boundaries) significantly affects retrieval quality in RAG systems, since chunks that are too large may dilute relevance while chunks that are too small may lose important context.

explainer.lead: Chunking breaks a long document into smaller pieces so each piece can be searched, stored, or passed to a model on its own. The way those pieces are sized and separated can determine whether a system finds the right information and keeps enough context to use it well.

tiers.eli5: Imagine trying to find one fact in a huge book. Instead of handing someone the whole book, you cut it into smaller passages that are easier to search through. If the passages are too big, the useful fact gets lost among unrelated words; if they are too tiny, they may not make sense without the sentences around them.
tiers.practitioner: In a RAG pipeline, chunk documents before indexing them, then tune chunk size, overlap, and boundary placement against retrieval quality. Overly large chunks can dilute relevance, while very small chunks can drop surrounding context needed to interpret a match. Check that important passages are not split at unhelpful boundaries.
tiers.paperLevel: Given a document D, chunking constructs an ordered sequence of segments C = (c1, c2, ..., cn), optionally with shared text between adjacent segments. Its main parameters are segment size, overlap, and boundary selection. In RAG, these parameters trade retrieval specificity against the preservation of context; there is no universally best chunk size stated here.

explainer.example: A support team splits a 40-page troubleshooting guide into 300-word passages with 40 words of overlap. A retrieval system can then return the passage about resetting a device without including the whole guide, while the overlap helps preserve instructions that cross a boundary.

usedIn.name: Retrieval-augmented generation
usedIn.detail: Documents are divided into retrievable passages whose size and overlap affect the relevance of retrieved context.

usedIn.name: Document indexing
usedIn.detail: Long texts are stored as smaller segments that can be processed and searched individually.

usedIn.name: Model context preparation
usedIn.detail: Selected passages can be included in a model's context instead of an entire long document.

explainer.intuition: A chunk should be small enough to focus on a useful part of a document, but large enough to preserve the meaning around it. Chunking is therefore a balancing act, not simply cutting text at a fixed interval.
howItWorks: Start with a document that is too long to process or include as a whole.
Choose a chunk size and decide where boundaries should fall.
Split the document into segments, adding overlap when neighboring chunks need shared context.
Process or index the chunks for later retrieval.
Place relevant retrieved chunks into the model's context.
explainer.whyItMatters: Chunking directly shapes what a retrieval system can find and what context a model receives. Poor choices can bury a relevant fact inside unrelated material or separate it from information needed to understand it.
misconceptions: Smaller chunks are not always better: they can lose essential surrounding context.
Bigger chunks are not automatically more informative: they can dilute relevance.
Chunking does not itself retrieve information or generate an answer; it prepares text for those later steps.

nodes.label: Model context
nodes.note: Selected text supplied to the model
